title: Act with the user's own access
glance: An agent that serves people should reach data with each person's own scoped access, not a shared all-powerful account; use a service identity only when no person is behind the request.
story: Authentication proves who someone is (signing in). Authorization decides what they may reach. They are different gaps: signing users in does not stop an agent from showing them data they may not see, if the agent fetches everything with one powerful account.

That shared account is the trap. It is quick to set up, but it means the agent can reach anything for anyone, and the only thing deciding what a user sees is the model, which is not an access control. The fix is delegated access: the agent calls the system with a token that carries the signed-in user's own permissions (for example through OAuth, which remote MCP servers support), so the system itself refuses what the user could not open.

Two lookalikes: when no person is behind the request, such as a scheduled job, there is no one to delegate from, so the job gets its own narrowly scoped service identity. And when users are not signed in at all, authentication has to come first, because authorization needs a known identity.
situation: A university's research-office assistant helps staff find grant documents on the shared drive. It searches with one service account that can read every folder. Staff sign in with single sign-on, and folder permissions differ by department. A lecturer received text from another department's confidential budget. What should the architect change?

options.t: Call the drive's search with the signed-in user's delegated, scoped token.
Add a system-prompt rule not to reveal documents from other departments.
Give the job its own service account, scoped to the folders it needs.
Make users sign in before they can use the assistant at all.

worlds.name: As written
worlds.fact: Staff are already signed in, and the drive already has per-user folder permissions.
worlds.why: The drive already knows what each person may open. Searching with the user's own token lets the drive enforce it.

losers.B: A prompt rule is not access control; the budget text still reaches the model.
losers.C: A narrower shared account still shows every user whatever that account can read.
losers.D: Users are already signed in; the gap is authorization, not authentication.

worlds.name: No person behind it
worlds.fact: The assistant is a nightly job, started by a schedule, that summarises new grant calls from two public-funding folders for a morning email.
worlds.why: There is no user to delegate from, so least privilege applies to the job: its own identity, able to read only those two folders.

losers.A: There is no signed-in user whose token the job could use.
losers.B: A prompt rule still leaves an account that can read every folder.
losers.D: Nobody signs in to a scheduled job.

worlds.name: Nobody is signed in
worlds.fact: The assistant is open on the intranet without sign-in, so anyone on the network can use it and it cannot tell who is asking.
worlds.why: Authorization needs a known identity. Authentication comes first; delegated access can follow.

losers.A: Without sign-in there is no user token to delegate.
losers.B: A prompt rule cannot tell which department an anonymous user is in.
losers.C: A scoped service account would still serve the same data to every anonymous user.

signals: “one service account” or “an admin account that can read everything”
“users already sign in with single sign-on”
a user saw data “they could not open themselves”
remember: If a person is behind the request, act with that person's own scoped access. If no person is, give the job its own narrow identity. If you do not know who is asking, fix sign-in first.

practice.stem: A hospital's scheduling assistant lets clinicians check and book operating-theatre slots. It calls the scheduling system with an integration account that sees every specialty's lists, although each clinician's own login sees only their specialty. A surgeon received another specialty's patient list. Clinicians already sign in with single sign-on. What should the architect change?
options: Call the scheduling system with each clinician's own delegated token.
Pass the clinician's specialty to the model and tell it to filter the results.
Record which clinician viewed which patient list in a detailed audit log.
Create one account per specialty, chosen by the specialty typed in the chat.
practice.why: The deciding facts: clinicians are signed in, and the scheduling system already enforces per-specialty access. A delegated token lets it apply those rules.
traps: Works most of the time, but the model is filtering data it should never have received.
Works for accountability, but it records the exposure instead of preventing it.
Works if the specialty were trusted, but anyone can type another specialty's name.

practice.stem: A bank has two legal entities, retail and investment, with a strict information barrier between them. Every employee belongs to exactly one, and all documents within an entity are open to its own staff. The bank's assistant searches one shared index with a crawler account. Staff sign in with single sign-on. What design fits best?
options: Keep the shared index and add a prompt rule naming the barrier.
Keep the shared index and log each answer with the asker's entity.
Build one index per entity, and search only the user's own entity's index.
Store each document's full access list on its chunks and filter every query.
practice.why: The deciding fact: access follows a clean split by entity, with everything open inside each one. Separate indexes, chosen from the signed-in user's entity, are simpler and enough.
traps: Works for tone, but a prompt is not an access control across a legal barrier.
Works for auditing, but it records breaches instead of stopping them.
Works, and would win if permissions varied document by document, but here they do not.

practice.stem: A note-taking assistant saves meeting summaries into each employee's cloud drive using the employee's own OAuth token. When it was set up, it requested full drive access, including deleting files and sharing them outside the company. It only ever creates new documents in one folder. What should the architect change?
options: Switch to one service account with write access to every employee's drive.
Request a narrower scope that lets it create files in the notes folder.
Keep full access, and log every deletion and external share it makes.
Keep full access, and ask the employee to confirm any external share.
practice.why: The deciding fact: the assistant only creates documents in one folder. Delegated access is right, but the scope it asks for should match the role.
traps: Works technically, but a shared account reaches every drive and loses per-user limits.
Works for audit, but it watches powers the assistant never uses.
Works when the role sometimes needs sharing, but this one never does.
